extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, policy makers, development practitioners, and journalists interested in climate-change communication
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing media coverage of climate change
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and conceptual criteria for assessing how news media produce, frame, and disseminate coverage of climate change (mitigation and adaptation), including multi-scale influences and journalistic norms. Useful for media studies analyses, policy assessment, and improving journalism practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing (selection and salience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing involves selection and salience: selecting some aspects of a perceived reality and making them more salient in a communicating text so as to promote a particular problem definition (Entman 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which elements of discourse are privileged or omitted, how issues are assembled into coherent narratives, and whether frames favor particular interpretations (e.g., political, economic). Example: Pielke Jr.'s observation about how definitional limits (UNFCCC's restricted definition of 'climate change') have policy implications. Consider structural and agential components that combine to produce frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization (first-order norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to focus on individuals (human-interest stories, personalities) rather than group dynamics or structural analysis, privileging competition between personalities over systemic explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether stories foreground individual claims-makers and personal drama at the expense of institutional, structural or socio-economic context. Note the tendency for such stories to lack linkage to deeper social analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization (first-order norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic dramatization values drama as the source of energy that gives social problems life and sustains their growth (Hilgartner and Bosk), favoring surface movement over comprehensive analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sensationalized or alarmist presentation ('climate porn') and whether dramatization downplays enduring causes and consequences. Example: Hurricane Katrina triggering a wave of coverage despite scientific uncertainty about links to climate change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / News Peg / 'Repetition taboo' (first-order norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists prefer fresh, original stories and often reject stories already reported (Gans' 'repetition taboo'), creating a bias toward crises or events with a clear 'news peg'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether chronic, creeping problems (long-term climate impacts, adaptation strategies) are sidelined because they lack novelty. Consider saturation effects where redundant claims can dedramatize an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority-order bias (second-order norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists tend to consult and privilege authority figures (government officials, business leaders) reflecting a desirability of social order and leadership (Gans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reliance on official/elite sources, and consider how this shapes problem definitions and public trust. Note how authority-order can defuse or amplify concern depending on contexts of contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance norm and false equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance—presenting views of conflicting sides with roughly equal attention—is used to pursue objectivity, but can produce 'dueling scientists' and give disproportionate weight to minority views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether balanced reporting results in divergence from scientific consensus (e.g., Boykoff & Boykoff 2004 finding 52.7% of prestige-press articles presented roughly equal attention to anthropogenic vs natural explanations). Consider whether balance obscures evidence-weighted judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic versus Thematic Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic framing treats issues as discrete events or individual cases, while thematic framing situates stories in larger contexts; episodic framing leads to shallower public understanding (Iyengar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify coverage as episodic or thematic and evaluate consequences for public comprehension of long-term climate processes and policy options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of scientific uncertainty and tendency to over-certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists communicate probabilities and caution; media often translate hypotheses into certainties and simplify cautious scientific language into unequivocal commentary (Weingart et al. 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess accuracy in reporting scientific uncertainty, whether probabilistic findings are overstated as certainties, and how translation choices affect public understanding and policy debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro political-economic influences on news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Core structural factors—pursuit of profit, firm size, competition, horizontal/vertical integration, advertising influence, owners' and managers' interests, and employee characteristics—shape media content (McChesney).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ownership and commercial structures, advertising pressures, consolidation, and how these factors bias coverage priorities or angles (e.g., privileging economic stability over environmental risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource constraints: deadlines, space, and budget
rubrics_metrics.description: Tight deadlines and space considerations constrain journalists, leading to reliance on few sources and limited ability to comprehend and communicate complex climate science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how time and budget pressures lead to shallow sourcing, reduced investigative reporting, and replication of wire-service material. Example: reliance on single sources due to deadlines (Dunwoody 1986).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' disciplinary background and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journalists lack formal training in science or math, reducing their ability to cover complex scientific topics effectively (Dunwoody & Peters 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporters' expertise, availability of science journalism training, and whether technical complexity is appropriately conveyed or overly simplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement, exposure, and editorial decisions (headlines, photos, front page vs buried)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial choices about exposure, placement, headlines and photographs influence how events are construed by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prominence (front-page vs buried), visual framing, and headline wording as vectors that amplify or minimize perceived importance and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire services' role in shaping frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services have played a key role in shaping how climate science is framed and discussed in reporting, often leading to reproduced, non-local narratives (Antilla 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check dependency on wire copy, degree of replication across outlets, and impacts on diversity of perspectives—particularly in Global South contexts where repurposed material dominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-scale pressures (political, economic, social, cultural, ethical, journalistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage is shaped by interconnected pressures across scales—from macro political-economy to micro journalistic practices—making influences complex and hard to disentangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider interactions among scales when diagnosing framing outcomes; avoid single-cause explanations and map feedback loops between production, public sphere, and individual engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention economy / Issue-Attention dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Public attention to environmental issues moves through stages (Downs' Issue-Attention Cycle): pre-problem, alarmed discovery, gradual realization of cost, decline of intense interest, and post-problem limbo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cycle to analyze rises and falls in coverage and public concern, but also recognise its limitations (linearity, partial explanatory power). Consider how media selection principles determine issue survival in public arenas (Hilgartner & Bosk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility of climate discourse in the public sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoded media messages (broadcasts, print, internet) compete in public arenas for attention; legibility depends on institutional, political and cultural principles of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how accessible, timely, and understandable climate information is to publics—whether messages are encoded in jargon or translated into clear, actionable narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jargon and clarity of scientific communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Low levels of knowledge among journalists are linked to lack of access to timely, clear and understandable information and the use of excessive jargon by scientists, NGOs and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sources provide clear, non-jargon explanations and whether intermediaries (press offices, NGOs) facilitate comprehensible messaging for journalists, especially in developing-country contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial resources and beat allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Insufficient financial resources limit first-hand reporting, training, and the ability to maintain dedicated 'green' beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure newsroom budgets, availability of specialist reporters, and resource allocations that affect depth and continuity of climate adaptation coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial priorities and market-driven selection ('what sells')
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and advertisers prefer stories that 'sell' (crime, violence), producing incongruent habits and priorities that reduce coverage of adaptation and other climate topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial decision-making incentives and the marketability calculus that deprioritizes long-term or less sensational climate stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback loops: media influence on science, policy and subsequent frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Media representations feed back into science-policy-public interactions over time, shaping subsequent news framing, science questions, and policy discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how media frames have influenced policy actors and scientific agendas (and vice versa), and consider temporal feedbacks when evaluating cause and effect in coverage trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global/regional disparities in coverage and repurposing of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of climate change and adaptation is substantially lower outside Europe and North America; many outlets in developing countries reproduce stories from Western sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the balance of locally produced vs repurposed content, the representation of local vulnerabilities (e.g., 'survival' vs 'luxury' emissions), and structural barriers to local science access and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling limitations and need for dynamic, non-linear analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Static, linear models (e.g., Downs' Issue-Attention Cycle) fail to capture contested terrains and non-linear interactions among media, science, and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying explanatory models, prefer frameworks (Circuits of Communication, Public Arenas) that account for dynamic feedbacks, contestation, and multi-actor competition for frames and attention.
